intro: In 1947 a shepherd's stone cracked a jar in a cave near the Dead Sea. That jar began a find of about 900 old manuscripts. One small scrap held a line from Deuteronomy 32:8. Its wording did not match the Hebrew Bible most people used. Where the usual text says the nations were divided by the number of the sons of Israel, the scroll says the sons of God.

That one verse opens a big question: who rules the nations? Deuteronomy 32, Daniel 10, Psalm 82, Sirach, Jubilees and 1 Enoch all give answers. In this unit you will read them, along with holy ground at Sinai and Zion and a general who carried Israel's soil home. Then you will meet the researchers who read these texts. Michael Heiser, Mark S. Smith, George Nickelsburg and others see them in different ways.

By the end of the unit you will be able to explain what a manuscript and a variant are, and compare the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls. You will be able to say what Deuteronomy 32, Daniel 10 and 2 Kings 5 say in your own words. And you will be able to describe two readings of each and compare them fairly.
bigQuestion: What do Deuteronomy 32, Daniel 10 and 2 Kings 5 say about the nations, their rulers and the land of Israel, and how have researchers read them?

timeline.t: Babylon destroys Jerusalem; exiles later ask how to sing the LORD's song in a strange land (Psalm 137)
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon; Daniel 10 is set in his third year
Alexander the Great defeats Persia; Greece follows Persia, as in Daniel's princes
Jews in Alexandria begin translating the Torah into Greek, the Septuagint
Ben Sira writes Sirach, which says God set a ruler over every people
Jubilees retells Genesis and says no angel rules over Israel
The Aleppo Codex, a Masoretic Hebrew Bible, is written
The Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible that survives, is finished
Digging begins at Ugarit in Syria; its tablets tell of the god El and his seventy sons
A Bedouin shepherd finds the first Dead Sea Scrolls near Qumran
Cave 4 is found; among its thousands of fragments is 4QDeut-j

words.d: a copy of a text written by hand
a place where two or more copies of a text do not agree
the traditional Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, guarded and marked by Jewish scribes called Masoretes
an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Alexandria in the 200s BCE
about 900 ancient Jewish manuscripts found in caves near Qumran from 1947 to 1956
in the Hebrew Bible, a phrase that can name heavenly beings, as in Job 1:6 and 38:7
Heiser's name for the idea that God gave the nations to lesser divine beings at Babel and kept Israel as his own
a rare Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 for spirit beings who received sacrifices
in Daniel 10, a ruler; the prince of Persia, the prince of Greece, and Michael, the prince of Daniel's people
the gathering of heavenly beings around God, pictured in Psalm 82 and 1 Kings 22
ground set apart for God because, in the story, God is present there
a share given to someone; in Deuteronomy 32:9, Israel is the LORD's portion

test.q: Which text of Deuteronomy 32:8 reads "sons of Israel"?
test.why: The Masoretic Text reads "sons of Israel"; the scroll reads "sons of God" and most Greek copies "angels of God."

test.q: What does the Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-j read in Deuteronomy 32:8?
test.why: 4QDeut-j, from Qumran Cave 4, reads "sons of God."

test.q: Why do scholars value the Septuagint when studying the Hebrew text?
choices: It is the oldest Hebrew codex
It was translated from Hebrew copies much older than the Masoretic codices
It was written by the Masoretes
test.why: The Greek translators worked from old Hebrew copies, so the Septuagint can show an older Hebrew reading.

test.q: Which statement about the Dead Sea Scrolls is correct?
choices: They are all copies of Isaiah
They were found in eleven caves near Qumran, 1947–1956
They were copied in about 1000 CE
test.why: The scrolls were found in eleven caves near Qumran between 1947 and 1956.

test.q: Which passages did Heiser link to build the Deuteronomy 32 worldview?
choices: Deuteronomy 32:8–9 and the Babel story in Genesis 10–11
test.why: Heiser read Deuteronomy 32:8–9 as looking back to Babel and the nations in Genesis 10–11.

test.q: Which Greek word did the Septuagint use for the gods of the nations in Psalm 96:5?
test.why: The Hebrew says elilim (idols); the Septuagint translated it daimonia.

test.q: In Daniel 10, what blocked the heavenly messenger for twenty-one days?
choices: The prince of the kingdom of Persia
test.why: Daniel 10:13 says the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood him twenty-one days.

test.q: Who does Daniel call the prince of Daniel's people?
test.why: Daniel 10:21 and 12:1 name Michael as the prince who stands for Daniel's people.

test.q: Which ancient Jewish book says God set a ruler over every people, but Israel is the Lord's portion?
test.why: Sirach 17:17 echoes Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in these words.

test.q: Besides heavenly rulers, how else have readers understood Daniel's princes?
choices: They read the princes as human officials or as symbols
They say the princes are Masoretes
They say Michael is the prince of Persia
They say Daniel is about Egypt
test.why: Some interpreters read the princes as human officials; some modern scholars read them as symbols of God's hand in history.

test.q: Why was the ground holy in Exodus 3:5?
choices: Because the Israelites built an altar there
Because, in the story, God was present there
test.why: Holy means set apart for God; the ground is holy because God speaks from the bush there.

test.q: Why do many scholars think Naaman asked for Israel's soil?
choices: Because a land was linked to its god, so he took the LORD's ground home
To make bricks for a palace
To grow Israel's crops in Aram
test.why: Many scholars see the soil as a way to worship Israel's God in Aram, since lands were tied to gods.

test.q: In 1 Samuel 26:19, what does David say being driven out of the LORD's inheritance is like?
choices: Being told to go serve other gods
test.why: David says it is as if they told him, "Go, serve other gods."

test.q: Which verse do readers often point to when they say God is not limited to one land?
test.why: Psalm 24:1 says the earth is the LORD's and everything in it.

test.q: In Psalm 48:2, Zion is "on the sides of the north." What name does the Hebrew word for north share?
choices: Zaphon, Baal's mountain in Ugarit's texts
test.why: The Hebrew word for north is tsaphon; Zaphon was Baal's mountain in Ugarit's texts, and many scholars read the psalm as claiming that honor for Zion.

write.prompt: Did the land of Israel matter for worship in the Bible? Use Deuteronomy 32:8–9, 2 Kings 5:17 and one more passage from this unit (such as 1 Samuel 26:19 or Psalm 24:1). Explain what each text says, how one researcher read it, and how at least one other reader sees it.
tips: Name each text by book, chapter and verse, and say which reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 you mean.
Attribute every idea: "Heiser argued...", "Smith read...", "the text says...".
Compare the readings fairly; do not rank them or say which one is true.
Use at least three unit terms, such as manuscript, variant, portion or holy ground.
Explain scholars' ideas in your own words; do not quote their books.
